```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "##", fig.align = "center",
                      fig.height = 4)
```

# Install NNS

We need the latest version of NNS available on GitHub.

```{r install}
# library(devtools); install_github('OVVO-Financial/NNS', ref = "NNS-Beta-Version")
library(NNS)
```

# Correlation

NNS nonlinear correlation is based on partial moment matrices. Partial moment
matrices reflect the relationship between variables. Using these topological
relations, we are able to avoid relying upon geometry for correlation. There
are only 4 relationships between 2 variables and each relationship is
represented by a partial moment matrix:

* $X \le$ target, $Y \le$ target $\rightarrow$ CLPM matrix
* $X \le$ target, $Y >$ target $\rightarrow$ DUPM matrix
* $X >$ target, $Y \le$ target $\rightarrow$ DLPM matrix
* $X >$ target, $Y >$ target $\rightarrow$ CUPM matrix

```{r quadrants, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 6}
set.seed(123)
qx <- rnorm(1000); qy <- rnorm(1000)
quad <- list("CLPM Quadrant" = qx <= 0 & qy <= 0, "DUPM Quadrant" = qx <= 0 & qy > 0,
             "CUPM Quadrant" = qx > 0 & qy > 0, "DLPM Quadrant" = qx > 0 & qy <= 0)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (q in names(quad)) {
  plot(qx, qy, col = ifelse(quad[[q]], "steelblue", "grey85"), pch = 19, cex = .5,
       xlab = "X", ylab = "Y", main = q)
  abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 2)
}
```

# Linear Equivalence

First, let's demonstrate NNS equivalence to Pearson's correlation coefficient
under a condition of perfect linearity.

```{r linear}
x = seq(-3, 3, .01); y = 2 * x
cor(x, y)
NNS.dep(x, y, print.map = TRUE)
```

Note how under perfect correlation, all of the observations are in the similar
CUPM and CLPM quadrants.

```{r inverse}
x = seq(-3, 3, .01); y = -2 * x
cor(x, y); NNS.dep(x, y, print.map = TRUE)
```

Note how under perfect inverse correlation, all of the observations are in the
divergent DUPM and DLPM quadrants.

# Nonlinear Examples

Now that you understand the relationship between the relationship matrices, we
can introduce some nonlinearity to the analysis.

```{r squared}
x = seq(0, 3, .01); y = x^2
cor(x, y); NNS.dep(x, y, print.map = TRUE)
```

Both methods report a high correlation for the previous gentle example.
Increasing the nonlinearity will reveal the deficiencies in the geometric
based linear approach.

```{r tenth}
x = seq(0, 3, .01); y = x^10
cor(x, y); NNS.dep(x, y, print.map = TRUE)
```

Again, even though the observations do not follow a straight line, they occur
primarily in the CUPM and CLPM quadrants, yielding a far higher NNS correlation
coefficient than Pearson's.

# Clustered Examples

In highly clustered datasets, linear correlation is essentially useless. Here
is an example showing 3 distinct clusters and the significant inverse
correlation Pearson's inappropriately assigns.

```{r clusters, eval = FALSE}
# The 2021 data link (https://goo.gl/AA6HMf) no longer resolves.
cluster.df <- read.csv("https://goo.gl/AA6HMf", header = FALSE, sep = '')
cor(cluster.df[, 3], cluster.df[, 4])
NNS.dep(cluster.df[, 3], cluster.df[, 4], print.map = TRUE)
```

In 2021 this printed a Pearson correlation of -0.6275592 against an NNS
correlation of -0.01117909 and dependence of 0.1079831.

# Dependence

The spherical distribution is the best example of the dependence technique.
Many cite it as a counter-example to the applicability of Pearson's
correlation when trying to determine the relationship between two variables.

```{r circle}
set.seed(123)
df <- data.frame(x = runif(10000, -1, 1), y = runif(10000, -1, 1))
df <- subset(df, (x^2 + y^2 <= 1 & x^2 + y^2 >= 0.95))
NNS.dep(df$x, df$y, print.map = TRUE)
```

While there is no correlation to speak of in this spherical distribution,
there is obvious dependence between $X$ and $Y$. This dependence is reported by
NNS.

A majority of observations are in either similar (CUPM, CLPM) partial moment
quadrants or divergent (DUPM, DLPM) quadrants.

Here is our earlier $y = x^2$ example, where the dispersion of the line affects
the dependence...

```{r noisy}
set.seed(123)
x = seq(0, 3, .01); y = x^2 + rnorm(length(x), sd = 1)
NNS.dep(x, y, print.map = TRUE)
```

# Multivariate Dependence

These partial moment insights permit us to extend the analysis to multivariate
instances. This level of analysis is simply impossible with Pearson or other
rank based correlation methods, which are restricted to bi-variate cases.

## Independent Case

First we present the independent case. In the 3-D plot below, the regions of
co-partial moments are shaded: green is the Co-UPM and red is the Co-LPM.
Under independence, we know that $2(.5^n)$ of the observations should occupy
these regions for $n$ dimensions. In our 3 variable normal example, the green
and red dots representing Co-UPM and Co-LPM observations respectively are
restricted to their appropriate regions.

```{r copula-independent}
set.seed(123)
x = rnorm(1000); y = rnorm(1000); z = rnorm(1000)
NNS.copula(cbind(x, y, z))
```

```{r copula-independent-plot, eval = FALSE}
# Interactive 3-D view (rgl)
NNS.copula(cbind(x, y, z), plot = TRUE, independence.overlay = TRUE)
```

The 2021 version printed 0.09571785 here. That value is not reproduced by the
current implementation, which gives the value above; it is a descriptive
finite-sample score, not a p-value or an independence threshold (see
`examples/example-corrections.md`).

## Dependent Case

In our dependent case, where all variables are equal, all of the observations
fall within the co-partial moment regions, exhibiting a co-correlation of 1.

```{r copula-equal}
y = x; z = x
NNS.copula(cbind(x, y, z))
```

In our second dependent case, we examine $y = x_1^2 \cdot x_2^2$ where $y$ is
clearly dependent upon both $x_1$ and $x_2$. In the 3-D plot there is an
abundance of green Co-UPM observations outside of the green Co-UPM
independence shaded region.

```{r copula-product}
x = seq(0, 1, .01); y = seq(0, 1, .01); B = expand.grid(x, y)
z = B[, 1]^2 * B[, 2]^2
NNS.copula(cbind(B, z))
```

# Significance

One question remaining is, how significant are these results? p-values can be
obtained from sampling random permutations of $y \rightarrow y_p$ and running
`NNS.dep(x, y_p)` to compare against a null hypothesis of 0 correlation or
independence between $(x, y)$.

```{r significance, fig.height = 3.5}
set.seed(123)
x = seq(-5, 5, .1); y = x^2 + rnorm(length(x))
NNS.dep(x, y, p.value = TRUE, print.map = TRUE)
```

We fail to reject the null hypothesis of 0 correlation between $(x, y)$.

We reject the null hypothesis of independence between $(x, y)$: our dependence
result lies far outside the distribution of permuted results.

> **Note (2026).** The quantiles of the permuted statistics describe a null
> reference distribution under exchangeability. They are not a confidence
> interval for the population correlation or dependence. For serial or
> clustered data, use a resampling scheme that preserves that structure (see
> `examples/example-corrections.md`).

# Key Takeaway

These examples illustrate the main point on dependence:

If $X$ and $Y$ are perfectly correlated or perfectly inversely correlated, they
are completely dependent upon one another.

# Other Considerations

Rank based correlations do not consider the area of the distribution. This
potentially ignores a lot of important information when trying to determine
the relationship between two variables. NNS has additional features to
consider the area of the joint distribution by altering its partial moment
degree, 0 for frequency and 1 for area.

Furthermore, correlation and dependence matrices are generated when a matrix
is entered into `NNS.dep()`. We refer readers to the NNS manual available on
CRAN: <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/NNS/NNS.pdf>

To learn more about NNS statistics and their theoretical foundations, see
*Nonlinear Nonparametric Statistics: Using Partial Moments*
(<https://ovvo-financial.github.io/NNS/book/>). More NNS examples are posted
on GitHub: <https://github.com/OVVO-Financial/NNS/tree/NNS-Beta-Version/examples>
